alphabet: Latin letters (some passages read as pronounceable pseudo-words) plus separate lines of only '0', '1', '.', and 'x' characters, possibly Morse-like, per Schmeh: 'the Rubin cryptogram contains lines consisting of zeroes, ones, periods and x's only. This might represent a Morse-like code.'

constraints.hypothesis_bauer: Craig Bauer's hypothesis (author of 'Unsolved!'): Rubin created a short real message and padded it with meaningless letters (nulls) chosen so the nulls themselves form pronounceable but not necessarily meaningful words; recovering the message would require identifying which letters are the nulls
constraints.hypothesis_nomenclator: the pronounceable non-words could instead be codewords in a personal nomenclator/codebook, a device Rubin's own history supports: 'Rubin had always had an interest in encrypted messages. He used a number of complicated codes to communicate with his friends'
constraints.case_context: 18-year-old Jewish chemistry student, found dead of cyanide poisoning in a ditch at Philadelphia International Airport 20 minutes after a witness saw him alive; a small box containing the encrypted message was attached to his abdomen; unclear whether suicide or homicide
constraints.companion_cases: Schmeh groups this with Somerton Man and Ricky McCormick as one of only three unsolved criminal cases he knows of where the victim left an undeciphered note

cheap_tests_in_order: 1. Fetch the 2018 (Bauer) reproduction image and run a blind transcription pass, since no typed transcription exists anywhere found in this repo; separately catalogue the pure-symbol (0/1/./x) lines as a distinct block from the letter passages. Cost $1-2, Sonnet.

2. Print-check Craig Bauer's 'Unsolved!' (the book that produced the better scan) for any transcription or partial reading already in print, via Google Books/HathiTrust/Internet Archive per the Access playbook, before running fresh cryptanalysis on a possibly-already-published text. Cost $1.

3. Once transcribed, test the Morse-hypothesis lines (0/1/./x only) as literal Morse code or a simple binary mapping directly against English, since this is nearly free to check exhaustively and would need no language corpus if it produces recognisable words. Cost under $1.
